summary:
Nevşehir province operates under Turkey's national legal framework. No province-specific ordinance, incident or court decision has been recorded for Nevşehir; the sources supporting this record are national in scope, and the assessment below is the national picture as encountered in a tourism district of Cappadocia, where a tourism economy sits alongside regional conservatism.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Openly LGBTI people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classed under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' being made public.

Since 2015 local authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches, with police using water cannon and tear gas on the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025. The packages would criminalize expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, and they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

Press reports in early 2026 said the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex'; the provision was not included in the year's judicial reform package.
tangentialFactors:
Cappadocia's tourism economy draws international visitors year-round, but the sources record no Nevşehir-specific incident, enforcement action or local ordinance affecting LGBTI people. The province's exposure is the national pattern: bans and dispersal of Pride events, prosecutions of participants, court-ordered dissolution of an LGBTI association, and repeated legislative proposals to criminalise LGBTI identity and expression.

The draft packages of 2025 and the early-2026 proposal on 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' did not become law, so the statutory position at the time of writing remains the 1858 decriminalisation and the 1988 legal gender recognition procedure, without anti-discrimination protection.
localsOnly:
Transgender residents of Nevşehir province can change their legal gender under the national procedure available since 1988, but no provincial service, shelter or complaint mechanism specific to LGBTI residents is recorded in the sources.

Local authorities nationwide have used their powers to ban Pride marches since 2015; no Nevşehir-specific Pride event or ban is documented.

Openly LGBTI Turkish citizens face the national military-service regime, in which declaring homosexuality triggers classification as a 'psychosexual illness', a requirement to provide photographic proof, and the risk that the resulting 'unfit report' is made public.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the three 2025 draft law packages or the early-2026 proposal on 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

No Nevşehir-specific data on policing, hate incidents, healthcare access or facility use for trans visitors was identified; the national assessment applies.
